{{short description|Theorem in quantum physics}}
[[File:Triangle diagram.svg|thumb|This triangle diagram vanishes by Furry's theorem in quantum electrodynamics.]]
In [[quantum electrodynamics]], '''Furry's theorem''' states that if a [[Feynman diagram]] consists of a closed loop of [[fermion]] lines with an odd number of vertices, its contribution to the [[scattering amplitude|amplitude]] vanishes. As a [[corollary]], a single [[photon]] cannot arise from the [[quantum vacuum state|vacuum]] or be absorbed by it. The theorem was first derived by [[Wendell H. Furry]] in 1937,<ref  name="Furry">{{Cite journal|last=Furry|first=W. H.|author-link=Wendell H. Furry|date=1937-01-15|title=A Symmetry Theorem in the Positron Theory|url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRev.51.125|journal=Physical Review|language=en|volume=51|issue=2|pages=125–129|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.51.125|bibcode=1937PhRv...51..125F |issn=0031-899X|url-access=subscription}}</ref> as a direct consequence of the [[conservation of energy]] and [[C-symmetry|charge conjugation symmetry]].

== Theory ==

Quantum electrodynamics has a number of [[symmetry (physics)|symmetries]], one of them being the [[discrete symmetry]] of charge conjugation. This acts on fields through a [[unitary operator|unitary]] charge conjugation operator <math>C</math> which anticommutes with the photon field <math>A_\mu(x)</math> as <math>CA^\mu(x) C^\dagger = -A^\mu(x)</math>, while leaving the vacuum state invariant <math>C|\Omega\rangle = |\Omega\rangle</math>. Considering the simplest case of the [[correlation function (quantum field theory)|correlation function]] of a single photon operator gives

:<math>
\langle \Omega|A^\mu(x)|\Omega\rangle = \langle \Omega|C^\dagger C A^\mu(x) C^\dagger C|\Omega\rangle = - \langle \Omega|A^\mu(x)|\Omega\rangle,
</math>

so this correlation function must vanish.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Peskin|first1=M.E.|author1-link=Michael Peskin|last2=Schroeder|first2=D.V.|date=1995|title=An Introduction to Quantum Field Theory|publisher=Westview Press|chapter=10|page=318|isbn=978-0-201-50397-5}}</ref> For <math>n</math> photon operators, this argument shows that under charge conjugation this picks up a factor of <math>(-1)^n</math> and thus vanishes when <math>n</math> is odd. More generally, since the charge conjugation operator also anticommutes with the vector current <math>j^\mu(x)</math>, Furry's theorem states that the correlation function of any odd number of [[On shell and off shell|on-shell or off-shell]] photon fields and/or currents must vanish in quantum electrodynamics.

Since the theorem holds at the [[non-perturbative]] level, it must also hold at each order in [[perturbation theory (quantum mechanics)|perturbation theory]].<ref>{{cite book|first=S.|last=Weinberg|author1-link=Steven Weinberg|title=The Quantum Theory of Fields: Foundations|publisher=Cambridge University Press|date=1995|chapter=10|volume=1|page=428|isbn=978-0-521-67053-1}}</ref> At leading order this means that any [[one-loop Feynman diagram|fermion loop]] with an odd number of vertices must have a vanishing contribution to the amplitude. An explicit calculation of these diagrams reveals that this is because the diagram with a fermion going clockwise around the loop cancels with the second diagram where the fermion goes anticlockwise. The vanishing of the three vertex loop can also be seen as a consequence of the [[renormalization|renormalizability]] of quantum electrodynamics since the bare [[Lagrangian (field theory)|Lagrangian]] does not have any counterterms involving three photons.<ref>{{cite book|last=Sterman|first=G.|author-link=George Sterman|date=1993|title=An Introduction to Quantum Field Theory|url=|doi=|location=|publisher=Cambridge University Press|chapter=11|pages=326–327|isbn=978-0-521-31132-8}}</ref>

== Applications and limitations ==

Furry's theorem allows for the simplification of a number of amplitude calculations in quantum electrodynamics.<ref>{{cite book|last=Berestetskii|first=V.B.|date=1982|title=Quantum Electrodynamics: Volume 4 (Course of Theoretical Physics)|url=|doi=|location=|publisher=Butterworth-Heinemann|chapter=8|pages=315–316|isbn=978-0-7506-3371-0}}</ref> In particular, since the result also holds when photons are off-shell, all Feynman diagrams which have at least one internal fermion loops with an odd number of vertices have a vanishing contribution to the amplitude and can be ignored. Historically the theorem was important in showing that the scattering of photons by an external field, known as [[Delbrück scattering]], does not proceed via a triangle diagram and must instead proceed through a box diagram.<ref name="Furry"/>

In the presence of a background charge density or a nonzero [[chemical potential]], Furry's theorem is broken, although if both these vanish then it does hold at [[Thermal quantum field theory|nonzero temperatures]] as well as at zero temperatures.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Majumder|first1=A.|last2=Bourque|first2=A.|last3=Gale|first3=C.|date=2004|title=Broken symmetries and dilepton production from gluon fusion in a quark gluon plasma|url=|journal=Phys. Rev. C|volume=69|issue=6|article-number=064901|doi=10.1103/PhysRevC.69.064901|pmid=|arxiv=hep-ph/0311178|bibcode=2004PhRvC..69f4901M |s2cid=118879778}}</ref> It also does not apply in the presence of a strong background [[magnetic field]] where photon splitting interactions <math>\gamma \rightarrow \gamma \gamma</math> are allowed, a process that may be detected in [[astrophysics|astrophysical]] settings such as around [[neutron star]]s.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Adler|first1=S.L.|author-link1=Stephen L. Adler|date=1971|title=Photon splitting and photon dispersion in a strong magnetic field|url=|journal=Annals of Physics|volume=67|issue=2|pages=599–647|doi=10.1016/0003-4916(71)90154-0|pmid=|arxiv=|bibcode=1971AnPhy..67..599A |s2cid=}}</ref> The theorem also does not hold when [[Weyl equation|Weyl fermions]] are involved in the loops rather than [[Dirac fermion]]s, resulting in non-vanishing odd vertex number diagrams. In particular, the non-vanishing of the triangle diagram with Weyl fermions gives rise to the [[chiral anomaly]], with the sum of these having to cancel for a quantum theory to be consistent.

While the theorem has been formulated in quantum electrodynamics, a version of it holds more generally. For example, while the [[Standard Model]] is not charge conjugation invariant due to [[weak interaction]]s, the fermion loop diagrams with an odd number of photons attached will still vanish since these are equivalent to a purely quantum electrodynamical diagram. Similarly, any diagram involving such loops as sub-diagrams will also vanish. It is however no longer true that all odd number photon diagrams need to vanish. For example, relaxing the requirement of charge conjugation and [[parity (physics)|parity]] invariance of quantum electrodynamics, as occurs when weak interactions are included, allows for a three-photon vertex term.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Delbourgo|first1=R.|author-link=Robert Delbourgo|date=1976|title=The three-photon vertex|url=|journal=J. Phys. G|volume=2|issue=11|page=787|doi=10.1088/0305-4616/2/11/003|pmid=|arxiv=|bibcode=1976JPhG....2..787D |s2cid=250863523}}</ref> While this term does give rise to <math> \gamma \rightarrow \gamma \gamma </math> interactions, they only occur if two of the photons are [[virtual particle|virtual]]; searching for such interactions must be done indirectly, such as through [[bremsstrahlung]] experiments from electron-positron collisions.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Basham|first1=C.L.|last2=Kabir|first2=P.K.|date=1977|title=Possible three-photon couplings|url=|journal=Phys. Rev. D|volume=15|issue=11|pages=3388–3393|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.15.3388|pmid=|arxiv=|bibcode=1977PhRvD..15.3388B |s2cid=}}</ref>

In non-Abelian [[Yang–Mills theory|Yang–Mills theories]], Furry's theorem does not hold since these involve noncommuting [[color charge]]s. For example, the quark triangle diagrams with three external [[gluon]]s are proportional to two different [[Lie algebra#Generators and dimension|generator]] [[trace (linear algebra)|traces]] <math>\text{tr}[T^aT^bT^c] \neq \text{tr}[T^aT^cT^b]</math> and so they do not cancel.<ref>{{cite book|last=Dissertori|first=G.|author-link=Günther Dissertori|date=2009|title=Quantum Chromodynamics High Energy Experiments and Theory|url=|doi=|location=|publisher=Oxford University Press|chapter=3|pages=85–86|isbn=978-0-19-956641-9}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Smolyakov|first=N. V.|date=1982|title=Furry theorem for non-abelian gauge Lagrangians|url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF01016449|journal=Theoretical and Mathematical Physics|language=en|volume=50|issue=3|pages=225–228|doi=10.1007/BF01016449|bibcode=1982TMP....50..225S |s2cid=119765674|issn=0040-5779|via=|url-access=subscription}}</ref> However, charge conjugation arguments can still be applied in limited cases such as to deduce that the triangle diagram <math>gg \rightarrow X</math> for a color neutral [[Spin (physics)|spin]] <math>1^-</math> [[boson]] vanishes.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Englert|first1=C.|last2=Hackstein|first2=C.|last3=Spannowsky|first3=M.|date=2010|title=Measuring spin and CP from semihadronic ZZ decays using jet substructure|url=|journal=Phys. Rev. D|volume=82|issue=11|article-number=114024|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.82.114024|pmid=|arxiv=1010.0676|bibcode=2010PhRvD..82k4024E |s2cid=48357670}}</ref>
